Moral Responsibility. The property of being a proper subject of moral blame, praise, and accountability for one's actions. It assumes an agent is the originator of an act and is subject to justified reward or punishment for it. The question of what grounds moral responsibility—whether free will, conscious choice, or other conditions—is one of philosophy's enduring puzzles.

Responsibility requires agency. The person acted, rather than merely being acted upon; they caused the outcome through their own choice or will. Most philosophers agree responsibility requires knowledge and intent: one cannot be blamed for an action done in ignorance or without conscious choice.

The free will requirement is central. Libertarians argue genuine freedom—the ability to do otherwise—is necessary for responsibility; without it, praise and blame seem unjust. Compatibilists argue moral responsibility is compatible with determinism. What matters is acting from one's own desires and deliberations, not whether those desires were determined.

Diminished responsibility cases reveal important constraints. Young children, the insane, and the coerced are not fully responsible because they lack mature agency or freedom of choice. Collective responsibility raises another question: can groups—corporations, nations, communities—be morally responsible? Debates over corporate and state accountability rest on this question.

Strawson's reactive attitudes approach grounds moral responsibility not in metaphysics but in the natural human responses—resentment, gratitude, indignation—that constitute a moral community. Luck and responsibility generate further debate. Philosophers question whether brute luck—circumstances beyond control—can undermine responsibility. A person born into poverty faces different options than a born heir.

Moral responsibility connects to free will, the metaphysical condition most take to be necessary. Freedom, agency and autonomy, is required for responsibility. Determinism challenges traditional responsibility and raises questions about accountability. Virtue ethics ties responsibility to character; virtuous agents are worthy of praise for their reliable, excellent choices. Kant grounded responsibility in the rational autonomy of the moral agent, in duty and dignity. Causality matters too; philosophers debate whether causal participation is sufficient for responsibility. And moral philosophy encompasses theories of right action, virtue, and what agents owe each other.
